findings.claim: Revised (2018) Common Rule: an IRB must have written procedures that ensure proposed changes are reported promptly, and that investigators follow the approved terms until the IRB has reviewed and approved any proposed change. The only exception is a change needed to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to the subject. The regulation contains no exception for administrative changes.
findings.verbatimText: (iii) Ensuring prompt reporting to the IRB of proposed changes in a research activity, and for ensuring that investigators will conduct the research activity in accordance with the terms of the IRB approval until any proposed changes have been reviewed and approved by the IRB, except when necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to the subject.
findings.notes: The 2018 text does NOT contain the phrase 'may not be initiated without IRB review and approval'. That wording belongs to 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4) and to pre-2018 45 CFR 46.103(b)(4)(iii). The task's item 1 wording therefore paraphrases the 2018 rule; it does not quote it. The substance is the same.

findings.claim: Pre-2018 Common Rule: the same requirement was at 46.103(b)(4)(iii), worded as 'may not be initiated without IRB review and approval'. It moved to 46.108(a)(3)(iii) in the 2018 revision.

sources.title: OHRP Annotated Comparison of Pre-2018 and 2018 Requirements

findings.notes: The designation is confirmed by several hhs.gov results. The exact pre-2018 wording appeared only inside search-engine summaries, so it is not quoted here. Cite this designation only for pre-2018 studies, and for all other research use 46.108(a)(3)(iii).

findings.claim: FDA counterpart: the IRB must follow written procedures ensuring that changes to approved research are not initiated without IRB review and approval, except where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to the human subjects. The paragraph designation is (a)(4).
findings.verbatimText: (4) for ensuring that changes in approved research, during the period for which IRB approval has already been given, may not be initiated without IRB review and approval except where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to the human subjects.
findings.notes: Within 56.108(a), item (3) covers prompt reporting of changes and item (4) covers no initiation without approval. As with 45 CFR 46, there is no administrative exception.

findings.claim: Under an IND, the investigator must promptly report all changes in the research activity to the IRB and must not make any change in the research without IRB approval, except where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to human subjects.
findings.verbatimText: The investigator shall also assure that he or she will promptly report to the IRB all changes in the research activity and all unanticipated problems involving risk to human subjects or others, and that he or she will not make any changes in the research without IRB approval, except where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to human subjects.
findings.notes: This places the obligation on the investigator ('any changes'), which complements the IRB-procedure obligation in 56.108(a)(4). It too has no administrative exception.

findings.claim: FDA's IRB FAQ states that protocol amendments must be reviewed and approved by the IRB before they are implemented, unless an immediate change is necessary to eliminate an apparent hazard to subjects.
findings.citation: FDA, Institutional Review Boards Frequently Asked Questions – Information Sheet (final guidance), citing 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4)
findings.verbatimText: Protocol amendments must receive IRB review and approval before they are implemented, unless an immediate change is necessary to eliminate an apparent hazard to the subjects (21 CFR 56.108(a)(4)).
findings.notes: The FAQ does not create an administrative-amendment category.

findings.claim: OHRP: investigators who want to modify ongoing IRB-approved research must submit the request to the IRB and receive approval before implementing it, unless the change is designed to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard. A change made for that reason without prior approval must be reported to the IRB promptly.
findings.citation: OHRP Investigator Responsibilities FAQs (citing 45 CFR 46.103(b)(4) pre-2018; now 46.108(a)(3)(iii))
findings.notes: Search summaries consistently showed this proposition. The exact FAQ sentence was not reproduced reliably enough to quote. The FAQ still cites the pre-2018 designation.

findings.claim: Revised Common Rule: an IRB may use expedited review for minor changes in previously approved research during the period for which approval is authorized. The 2018 rule removed the pre-2018 qualifier '(of one year or less)'.
findings.verbatimText: Minor changes in previously approved research during the period for which approval is authorized

sources.title: OHRP 2018 Requirements guidance (cites §46.110(b)(1)(ii) for expedited review of minor consent changes)

findings.notes: The pre-2018 designation was 46.110(b)(2), 'during the period (of one year or less)'. That wording was not seen verbatim in a primary result; see unresolved.

findings.claim: FDA counterpart: an IRB may use expedited review for minor changes in previously approved research during the period (of 1 year or less) for which approval is authorized. FDA kept the '(of 1 year or less)' qualifier.
findings.verbatimText: (b) An IRB may use the expedited review procedure to review either or both of the following: (1) Some or all of the research appearing on the list and found by the reviewer(s) to involve no more than minimal risk, (2) minor changes in previously approved research during the period (of 1 year or less) for which approval is authorized.
findings.notes: Items (1) and (2) are inline in the running text of paragraph (b). By convention the minor-change route is cited as 56.110(b)(2).

findings.claim: Under expedited review, the IRB chairperson or one or more experienced IRB members designated by the chair do the review. They may exercise every IRB authority except disapproval. Disapproval is possible only after convened (non-expedited) review.
findings.verbatimText: Under an expedited review procedure, the review may be carried out by the IRB chairperson or by one or more experienced reviewers designated by the chairperson from among members of the IRB. In reviewing the research, the reviewers may exercise all of the authorities of the IRB except that the reviewers may not disapprove the research. A research activity may be disapproved only after review in accordance with the nonexpedited procedure set forth in § 46.108(b).
findings.notes: The text is high confidence. The paragraph label '(b)(2)' for the 2018 rule was not seen attached to this text, so the designation is medium. The FDA version refers to § 56.108(c).

findings.claim: Except when expedited review is used, the IRB must review proposed research at a convened meeting where a majority of members are present, including at least one member whose primary concerns are nonscientific. Approval requires a majority of the members present. A change that is not minor therefore goes to the convened IRB.
findings.verbatimText: Except when an expedited review procedure is used (as described in § 46.110), an IRB must review proposed research at convened meetings at which a majority of the members of the IRB are present, including at least one member whose primary concerns are in nonscientific areas. In order for the research to be approved, it shall receive the approval of a majority of those members present at the meeting.
findings.notes: The FDA text at 56.108(c) reads 'Except when an expedited review procedure is used (see § 56.110), review proposed research at convened meetings at which a majority of the members of the IRB are present, including at least one member whose primary concerns are in nonscientific areas.' Neither 46.108(b) nor 56.108(c) says 'major change → convened'. The result follows because expedited review is authorised only for minor changes, or for research that as amended still falls under 46.110(b)(1)(i) / 56.110(b)(1).

findings.claim: The IRB decides whether a change is minor. OHRP accepts a sponsor's (CTEP's) assessment that changes are minor only if the IRB chair or designated expedited reviewer agrees. If the chair or designee does not agree, the convened IRB must review the change. When new risk information is involved, the IRB must decide whether the approval criteria in 45 CFR 46.111, especially 46.111(a)(1) and (a)(2), are still met.
findings.citation: OHRP, IRB Review of Protocol and Informed Consent Changes for NCI/CTEP-Sponsored Clinical Trials (memo to Dr. Jeffrey Abrams, September 29, 2008)
findings.notes: The proposition is consistent across hhs.gov results. The exact sentences were not reproduced verbatim, so none are quoted. Consequence for the product: the sponsor's 'minor'/'administrative' label is advisory, and the IRB determines the review path. The memo also shows that a consent-form change adding new risk information CAN be minor if the IRB chair agrees, so 'affects consent' does not automatically mean 'not minor'. The memo predates the 2018 rule, but the 46.111 and 46.110 concepts are unchanged.

findings.claim: OHRP recommends that institutions adopt policies setting out which changes to approved research count as 'minor' and may be approved by expedited review, as distinct from changes greater than minor, which require review at a convened IRB meeting.
findings.citation: OHRP, Guidance on IRB Continuing Review of Research (November 2010)
findings.notes: Seen only in search summaries, and it was not possible to confirm which section of the 2010 guidance holds it. The guidance predates the 2018 rule, but OHRP has not withdrawn it.

findings.claim: Joint OHRP/FDA guidance on IRB written procedures says the procedures should address what might qualify as a minor change, the documents submitted for changes, and the type of review (full board or expedited). It repeats that changes may not be initiated without IRB review and approval except to eliminate apparent immediate hazards. The guidance was issued May 2018, replaced OHRP's 2011 written-procedures guidance, and was reissued in 2025.
findings.citation: OHRP/FDA, Institutional Review Board (IRB) Written Procedures: Guidance for Institutions and IRBs (final, May 2018; reissued 2025)
findings.notes: Seen through search summaries only. The reissue date is given as June 2025 on the HHS page and 'feb_2025' in the PDF filename. Neither date could be confirmed directly. The guidance leaves the definition of 'minor' to each IRB's written procedures, and nothing seen indicates that it creates an administrative category exempt from review.

findings.claim: SACHRP recommended defining minor changes that may be approved by expedited review as changes that neither materially increase risk, nor materially decrease benefit, nor materially decrease scientific merit. SACHRP is an advisory committee to the HHS Secretary. Its recommendations are not OHRP guidance and are not binding.
findings.citation: SACHRP Recommendation regarding definition of a minor change in research under 45 CFR 46 and 21 CFR 56 (approved July 20, 2011; Attachment B to Oct 13, 2011 letter)
findings.verbatimText: minor changes in approved research that can be approved through expedited review procedures are changes that neither materially increase risk, nor materially decrease benefit, nor materially decrease scientific merit

sources.title: SACHRP 2011 Attachment B (hosted on hhs.gov; advisory)

findings.notes: This is on the hhs.gov domain, but SACHRP is advisory, so it has less authority than OHRP guidance. The quoted sentence appeared consistently in several results. The fuller text and examples were not seen. A related SACHRP document (2013 expedited-review recommendations) describes FDA as treating any change that increases risk as not minor, and OHRP as treating changes that materially affect the risk/benefit assessment as not minor. That description was seen only in a summary. Product consequence: a change that DECREASES risk (for example deleting a research biopsy) can still be minor, so 'affectsRisk' must mean 'increases risk or adversely alters risk/benefit', not 'touches risk'.

findings.claim: FDA indicates that an IRB may use expedited review for consent-form changes that reflect minor changes to the protocol or recruitment plan. Example: a new advertisement that reuses wording from the approved consent form. A consent change is therefore not per se a non-minor change.
findings.citation: FDA, Institutional Review Boards Frequently Asked Questions – Information Sheet
findings.notes: Seen only in a search summary, and the FAQ item number is not confirmed. A statement that an unsure reviewer should consult the chair and send the change to the convened IRB was also summarised. The exact phrase could not be found or attributed to a specific FDA document, so it is not relied on.

findings.claim: ICH E6(R2) is the only source found that describes an 'administrative' category exempt from prior IRB/IEC approval. It is guidance, not regulation. Neither the investigator nor the IRB/IEC should allow deviations from or changes to the protocol without prior IRB/IEC approval, except to eliminate immediate hazards or when the change involves only logistical or administrative aspects of the trial, for example a change of monitor or telephone number.
findings.citation: ICH E6(R2) sections 3.3.7 and 4.5.2 (Step 4 Nov 2016; FDA guidance March 2018)
findings.verbatimText: or when the change(s) involves only logistical or administrative aspects of the trial (e.g., change in monitor(s), change of telephone number(s))
findings.notes: FDA adopted E6(R2) as non-binding guidance. It cannot override 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4) or 312.66, or 45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii), none of which contains this exception. At most, a purely logistical item that is not part of the IRB-approved research (such as a sponsor's monitor name) may not be a 'change in approved research' at all. That is a question for the IRB's written procedures, not a regulatory exemption.

findings.claim: ICH E6(R3) (Step 4, 6 January 2025) keeps the logistical/administrative exception in the IRB/IEC section. According to secondary summaries it now qualifies it with 'in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements'. In the US the applicable requirements (56.108(a)(4), 312.66, 46.108(a)(3)(iii)) provide no such exception. FDA issued E6(R3) as final guidance in September 2025.
findings.citation: ICH E6(R3) Annex 1, section 1.4.7 (designation unconfirmed); FDA guidance 'E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice (GCP)' (September 2025)

sources.title: ICH E6(R3) Step 4 Final Guideline (6 Jan 2025)

findings.notes: Neither the clause number 1.4.7 nor the qualifier 'in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements' was seen verbatim, and the matching investigator clause in E6(R3) section 2 was not found. Do not cite E6(R3) clause numbers in product text until someone checks them against the PDF. One summary gave the FDA issue date as 9/9/2025; it is not confirmed.

findings.claim: Re-consent: under both the Common Rule and FDA rules, when appropriate, subjects must be told of significant new findings developed during the research that may relate to their willingness to continue. Neither regulation uses the term 're-consent'. Whether and how enrolled subjects receive new information or are re-consented is decided by the IRB, not by the sponsor or the platform.
findings.verbatimText: A statement that significant new findings developed during the course of the research that may relate to the subject's willingness to continue participation will be provided to the subject

sources.title: SACHRP 2020 Attachment A – New Information Provided to Previously Enrolled Subjects (advisory)

findings.notes: The FDA text at 50.25(b)(5) reads '...which may relate to the subject's willingness to continue participation will be provided to the subject.' The platform must not treat 'affects consent' as meaning 're-consent required', and it must not claim a regulation requires re-consent. The correct output is that re-consent must be assessed and that the IRB determines it.

findings.claim: IRB practice (secondary source): large central IRBs require even trivial changes, such as a site phone number, to be reviewed and approved before implementation. The IRB, not the submitter, sorts changes into minor (expedited, single reviewer) and significant (convened board). Some institutions label a subset of minor changes 'administrative' (editorial fixes, personnel changes) and process them under their written procedures. That is still an IRB procedure, usually expedited review or staff acknowledgment under IRB policy. It is not an exemption from IRB review.
findings.citation: Secondary practice: Advarra, WCG IRB, institutional HRPP policies

sources.title: Advarra – IRB Review of Changes to Previously Approved Research

findings.notes: Advarra (summary): 'Prior to implementation, the IRB must review and approve any modification ... These changes can range from minor (e.g., updating the site's phone number) to significant.' WCG (summary): 'regulations require that any changes to the proposed study plan must be reviewed and approved by the IRB in advance' but formatting and administration are flexible. Practice varies by institution.

findings.claim: Devices: an IDE sponsor must obtain FDA approval of a supplemental application, and IRB approval 'when appropriate', before implementing a change to the investigational plan. Paragraphs (a)(2)–(a)(4) set out FDA-notification exceptions.
findings.notes: This is only relevant if the platform handles IDE studies. Whether 'when appropriate' interacts with 56.108(a)(4) to let any device change proceed without IRB approval was not researched. The IRB-level requirement in 56.108(a)(4) still applies to device studies under FDA IRB oversight.

research.determination:
Mapping rules for classifyAmendmentImpact (US), with the finding behind each:

R0. No US path skips IRB review. Every change to approved research, whatever its type, needs IRB review and approval before it is implemented (45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii); 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4); 21 CFR 312.66; FDA IRB FAQ). The only exception: a change needed to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to subjects may be made first and must then be reported to the IRB promptly.
- Model this as a separate flag (for example `immediateHazard: true`) that allows implementation and creates a prompt-report obligation.
- It must not be modelled as an amendment type.
- The platform must block the 'implemented' status until an IRB approval is recorded, for every type.

R1. amendmentType='major', whatever the flags → reviewPath 'convened' (the current 'full'). Expedited review is authorised only for minor changes (46.110(b)(1)(ii); 56.110(b)(2)). All other review happens at a convened meeting with a majority of members present, including one nonscientist, and approval by a majority of those present (46.108(b); 56.108(c)).
- The basis may add that research which as amended still qualifies under 46.110(b)(1)(i) / 56.110(b)(1) (minimal risk and on the expedited list) may be expedited. The classifier has no input for this, so defaulting to convened is correct.

R2. affectsRisk=true, any type → 'convened'. A change that materially increases risk or adversely changes the risk/benefit balance is not minor (SACHRP 2011, advisory; OHRP 2008 memo, 46.111(a)(1)-(2)).
- The flag must mean "increases risk or adversely alters risk/benefit". A risk-reducing change can be minor.

R3. affectsConsent=true with type minor or administrative and affectsRisk=false: no regulation requires convened review. Consent changes can be minor (FDA IRB FAQ; OHRP 2008 memo).
- Accurate output: reviewPath 'expedited', with a note that the IRB chair or designee decides whether the change is minor and refers it to the convened board if not (46.110(b)(2); 56.110(b)).
- If the product keeps 'convened' as a conservative default, the basis must say it is a platform policy and not a regulatory requirement.

R4. type='minor', affectsConsent=false, affectsRisk=false → 'expedited' under 46.110(b)(1)(ii) / 56.110(b)(2).
- The IRB chair or designated experienced member reviews it and may approve or require modifications, but may not disapprove.
- Disapproval requires convened review (46.110(b)(2); 56.110(b)).
- Whether the change is 'minor' is the IRB's decision, not the sponsor's (OHRP 2008 memo; OHRP/FDA IRB Written Procedures guidance).

R5. type='administrative', affectsConsent=false, affectsRisk=false → the same regulatory path as R4: IRB review required, eligible for expedited review as a minor change.
- The output must never say 'no IRB review' or allow implementation without a recorded IRB action.
- No US regulation or OHRP/FDA guidance defines an exempt 'administrative' category.
- The ICH E6(R2) 3.3.7 / 4.5.2 exception for logistical or administrative changes (monitor, phone number) is guidance. E6(R3) reportedly limits it to cases 'in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements', and the US requirements have no such exception.
- If the type must stay visible, keep reviewPath 'expedited' and add `sponsorLabel: 'administrative'`. Alternatively use a path value such as 'expedited_or_irb_procedure' whose basis says the IRB may handle it under its written procedures (for example acknowledgment), but that this is still IRB review.

R6. Undeclared flags.
- type='major' → 'convened'.
- type minor or administrative with a null flag → 'undetermined'. The current behaviour is correct, but the basis must cite 46.108(b) / 56.108(c) and 46.110(b)(1)(ii) / 56.110(b)(2), not 46.109.
- affectsRisk=true with the other flag null → 'convened'.

R7. Re-consent is never decided by the platform.
- Set `requiresReconsent`/`reconsentAssessmentRequired` = true when affectsConsent or affectsRisk is true; null when undeclared; false only when both are declared false.
- The basis must say the IRB decides whether and how enrolled subjects receive significant new findings or are re-consented (45 CFR 46.116(c)(5); 21 CFR 50.25(b)(5)). Neither regulation mandates 're-consent' as such.

Citation strings:
- IRB_REVIEW_REQUIRED: '45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii); 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4); 21 CFR 312.66 — a change to approved research must be reviewed and approved by the IRB before it is implemented, except when necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to subjects'
- EXPEDITED_BASIS: '45 CFR 46.110(b)(1)(ii); 21 CFR 56.110(b)(2) — minor changes in previously approved research during the period for which approval is authorized may be reviewed by expedited procedure (IRB chair or designated experienced member); the reviewer may not disapprove, and whether the change is minor is the IRB's determination'
- CONVENED_BASIS: '45 CFR 46.108(b); 21 CFR 56.108(c) — changes that are not minor are reviewed at a convened meeting with a majority of members present, including at least one nonscientist, and require approval by a majority of those present'
- ADMIN_BASIS: 'Sponsor-labelled administrative change. No US regulation or OHRP/FDA guidance exempts a change to approved research from IRB review (45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii); 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4); 21 CFR 312.66). It may be reviewed as a minor change by expedited procedure (45 CFR 46.110(b)(1)(ii); 21 CFR 56.110(b)(2)) or handled under the IRB's written procedures. The ICH E6 logistical/administrative exception is guidance and does not override these regulations.'
- RECONSENT_BASIS: '45 CFR 46.116(c)(5); 21 CFR 50.25(b)(5) — significant new findings that may relate to willingness to continue must be provided to subjects; whether and how enrolled subjects are re-consented is an IRB determination'
codeDefects: server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:6-8 — the header still cites '45 CFR 46.109(c) (continuing/amendment review)'. 46.109(c) covers documentation of informed consent. The amendment-review requirement is 46.108(a)(3)(iii) / 56.108(a)(4), and convened review is 46.108(b) / 56.108(c). The FULL_BASIS correction was not carried into the header.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:54-56 — the docstring says 'Administrative changes need neither'. 45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii), 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4) and 21 CFR 312.66 require IRB review and approval of every change before implementation, with no administrative exception.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:41,76 — reviewPath 'administrative' is not a US IRB review path. Returning it (with requiresReconsent false) for type 'administrative' with both flags false reads as 'no IRB review'. It should map to the expedited minor-change route (46.110(b)(1)(ii); 56.110(b)(2)), with the sponsor's label kept as metadata.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:24-28 and :30 (ADMIN_BASIS) — the comment treats 'can an administrative path mean no IRB review' as an open IRB-procedure question, and ADMIN_BASIS says 'whether it needs IRB review ... is for the IRB'. The regulations answer this: IRB review is required. The IRB decides only the procedure (expedited or convened) and whether an item is a change to approved research at all.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:29 (FULL_BASIS) — it says substantive changes 'affecting consent' go to the convened board as if a regulation required it. A consent change can be minor and expedited (FDA IRB FAQ; OHRP 2008 memo). It also does not cite 46.108(b) / 56.108(c), the actual convened-review provisions, and it wrongly attributes the 'may not be initiated' wording to 46.108(a)(3)(iii).

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:17 (EXPEDITED_BASIS) — it cites 46.110 / 56.110 with no paragraph. It should cite 45 CFR 46.110(b)(1)(ii) and 21 CFR 56.110(b)(2), and say that the IRB decides whether a change is minor and that an expedited reviewer cannot disapprove.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:48 (UNDECLARED_BASIS) — it cites '45 CFR 46.109 / 46.116; 21 CFR 56.110' for convened-board review. Convened review is 45 CFR 46.108(b) / 21 CFR 56.108(c). 46.109 is the IRB's general review authority.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:60-67 — any affectsConsent===true forces reviewPath 'full' and requiresReconsent true. Neither follows from regulation. Re-consent is an IRB determination under 46.116(c)(5) / 50.25(b)(5), and a consent change can be minor. affectsRisk has no direction, but only an increase in risk or an adverse change in risk/benefit makes a change non-minor; a risk reduction can be minor.

server/services/protocol-amendments/substantiality.ts:331 — the user-facing text asserts 'An administrative amendment is one that does not alter the risk/benefit assessment.' No regulation or OHRP/FDA guidance defines an administrative amendment. The nearest definition is SACHRP's advisory definition of a minor change ('neither materially increase risk, nor materially decrease benefit, nor materially decrease scientific merit').

server/services/protocol-amendments/substantiality.ts:5-6 — the module note says classifyAmendmentImpact 'is correct and it stays'. It is not correct for the 'administrative' and 'affectsConsent' branches, per the defects above.

server/services/irb/lifecycle.ts:100 (B_MOD) — the wording 'may not be initiated without IRB review and approval' comes from 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4) and pre-2018 45 CFR 46.103(b)(4)(iii), not from 46.108(a)(3)(iii). Also, 'an immediate hazard' should read 'apparent immediate hazards'. The substance is right, but the string should not be presented as a quote of 46.108(a)(3)(iii).

server/services/protocol-amendments/__tests__/protocol-amendments-logic.test.ts:24 — the test asserts the full-review basis matches /46\.109|46\.116/, which ties it to the wrong citation. It should assert 46.108(b) / 56.108(c) and 46.108(a)(3)(iii) / 56.108(a)(4).

server/services/protocol-amendments/__tests__/protocol-amendments-logic.test.ts:39-44 — the test locks in a separate 'administrative' reviewPath with no IRB-review requirement, which contradicts 56.108(a)(4) / 46.108(a)(3)(iii). Lines 27-31 and 46-49 lock in 'consent affected → full + re-consent true' as if it were a regulatory rule.

findings.claim: Introductory text of 21 CFR 312.30: once an IND is in effect, the sponsor has a general duty to amend it as needed so that the studies are conducted according to protocols contained in the application. This duty applies even where no specific (b)(1) trigger is met.
findings.verbatimText: Once an IND is in effect, a sponsor shall amend it as needed to ensure that the clinical investigations are conducted according to protocols included in the application.

sources.title: IND Application Reporting: Protocol Amendments | FDA

findings.notes: An exact-phrase search matched eCFR and the FDA page. The rest of the introductory text (the separate IND required for 50.24 emergency research) was not checked.

findings.claim: New protocol (a study not covered by a protocol already in the IND): the sponsor submits a protocol amendment containing the protocol. The study may begin once (1) the protocol has been submitted to FDA for review and (2) the IRB has approved it under part 56, in either order. 312.30 imposes no FDA approval and no waiting period.
findings.verbatimText: Such study may begin provided two conditions are met: (1) The sponsor has submitted the protocol to FDA for its review; and (2) the protocol has been approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) with responsibility for review and approval of the study in accordance with the requirements of part 56. The sponsor may comply with these two conditions in either order.

research.determination:
Rules for an FDA-submission classifier, kept separate from the IRB review path. Apply them only when the study is under a US IND. Where IND status is not recorded, return 'undetermined', never 'not required'.

R1. NEW PROTOCOL (a study not already covered in the IND)
- Output: 'Protocol Amendment: New Protocol'.
- The study may begin once BOTH have happened, in either order:
  - the protocol has been submitted to FDA;
  - the IRB has approved it.
- There is no FDA approval and no waiting period under 312.30 (21 CFR 312.30(a), 312.30(e)).

R2. CHANGE IN PROTOCOL: whether FDA submission is required depends on phase, which the classifier must take as an input (21 CFR 312.30(b)(1)).
- Phase 1: required only when the change significantly affects subject safety.
- Phase 2 or 3: required when the change significantly affects subject safety, the scope of the investigation, or the scientific quality of the study.
- Phase not recorded, or a combined Phase 1/2 study: apply the Phase 2/3 test and flag it. This is a conservative default; no primary text settles it.

R3. HARD TRIGGERS: return 'FDA submission required' whatever label the sponsor chose (21 CFR 312.30(b)(1)(i)–(iii)).
- (a) ANY increase in dose, or ANY increase in individual subjects' duration of exposure, beyond the current protocol. There is no significance qualifier, so no judgment is needed.
- (b) Adding or dropping a control group, or another significant design change.
- (c) Adding a test or procedure to monitor for, or reduce the risk of, an adverse event.
- (d) Dropping a test intended to monitor safety.
- An INCREASE in the number of subjects is a trigger only if it is 'significant'. The regulation sets no number, so the classifier reports the magnitude and asks for the sponsor's recorded judgment (312.30(b)(1)(i)). Do not invent a threshold.
- A DECREASE in the number of subjects is NOT a (b)(1)(i) example. It is relevant only through the general Phase 2/3 'scope / scientific quality' test, and then only as a sponsor judgment.

R4. IMPLEMENTATION GATE for a change that requires submission (21 CFR 312.30(b)(2)(i)):
- It may be implemented only when both are recorded, in either order:
  - the FDA submission;
  - IRB approval.

R5. IMMEDIATE HAZARD: a change made to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard (21 CFR 312.30(b)(2)(ii); 312.66; 56.108(a)(4)):
- may be implemented at once;
- then FDA must be notified by protocol amendment, and the IRB notified per 21 CFR 56.104(c).

R6. TIMING
- New protocols and protocol changes: submit before implementation (21 CFR 312.30(e)).
- New investigator: 'Protocol Amendment: New Investigator'. The investigator may start once added, and FDA must be notified within 30 days. These amendments may be grouped at 30-day intervals.
- Exception: no amendment is needed for a licensed practitioner added to a 312.315/312.320 treatment protocol (21 CFR 312.30(c), 312.30(e)).

R7. CONTENT: every submission must be prominently labelled with one of the three 312.30(d) titles. A change in protocol carries (21 CFR 312.30(d)):
- a brief description of the change;
- the date and number of the submission that contained the protocol;
- any supporting technical references;
- optionally, questions for FDA.

R8. BELOW THE THRESHOLD
- No 312.30(b) amendment is required.
- Phase 1: any 'significant Phase 1 protocol modification' not already reported goes in the next IND annual report (21 CFR 312.33(e) — paragraph (e), not (d); 312.23(a)(6)).
- Phase 2/3: Part 312 has no express slot. The classifier should say 'not required by 312.30(b)(1); sponsor may submit' rather than 'no FDA action'. The sponsor's general duty to keep the IND protocol current still applies (21 CFR 312.30 introductory text).

R9. IRB REVIEW IS INDEPENDENT AND ALWAYS REQUIRED (21 CFR 312.66; 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4))
- Every change needs IRB review and approval before it is initiated, except to eliminate apparent immediate hazards.
- The investigator must promptly report all changes and unanticipated problems to the IRB.
- 'Not required for FDA' therefore never means 'no IRB review'.

R10. MAPPING THE SPONSOR'S LABELS
The labels major, minor and administrative are the sponsor's vocabulary, not FDA categories:
- 'major': default to 'FDA submission required (Change in Protocol) before implementation', unless the study is Phase 1 and the sponsor records that the change does not significantly affect safety.
- 'minor': IRB expedited review does NOT settle the FDA question (56.110(b) versus 312.30(b)(1)).
  - Any R3 hard trigger makes submission required.
  - Otherwise the output is 'sponsor determination under 312.30(b)(1) required'.
- 'administrative': by definition it does not affect safety, scope or scientific quality, so it is 'not required by 312.30(b)(1)'.
  - Phase 1: consider 312.33(e).
  - IRB review is still required (R9).
  - Any R3 trigger contradicts the 'administrative' label and must surface as a declaration conflict.

R11. The existing stance on substantiality is correct: 'the sponsor judges significance and there is no numeric threshold' (312.30(b)(1), (b)(1)(i)). But it applies only to the subject-number and design-change examples. The dose and duration example is unconditional.

findings.claim: The 2023 FDA guidance also says the regulations do not define 're-consent' and do not set a process for informing enrolled subjects, so IRBs have flexibility.
findings.citation: FDA, Informed Consent: Guidance for IRBs, Clinical Investigators, and Sponsors (final, August 2023)
findings.verbatimText: FDA regulations do not use or define the term re-consent, nor do FDA regulations specify the process an IRB should use to determine the need or method to inform subjects who are already enrolled in the study of the new information. As such, IRBs have flexibility to establish procedures they think are appropriate to provide for subjects to have an opportunity to affirm their willingness to continue in the research.
findings.notes: Several secondary sources quote this and attribute it to the 2023 guidance. I did not see it in an fda.gov result.

findings.claim: The 2023 FDA guidance gives cases where new information need not go to previously enrolled subjects: a subject who has completed active participation, and information unlikely to affect willingness to continue. It allows other methods, such as a consent addendum or an information sheet, which the enrolled subject should be asked to sign and date.
findings.citation: FDA, Informed Consent: Guidance for IRBs, Clinical Investigators, and Sponsors (final, August 2023)
findings.verbatimText: such as a consent addendum or information sheet ... the enrolled subject should be asked to sign and date the consent addendum or information sheet
findings.notes: Only secondary summaries showed this. The exceptions are paraphrased, not quoted.

findings.claim: FDA's IRB FAQs (Information Sheet guidance on fda.gov) say which subjects must be told about a protocol change. Currently enrolled, actively participating subjects must be informed if the change might relate to their willingness to continue. Re-consent is not required for subjects who have completed active participation, or for changes that do not affect a subject's participation, such as changes that apply only to subjects enrolled later.
findings.citation: FDA, Institutional Review Boards Frequently Asked Questions – Information Sheet (informed consent FAQ citing 21 CFR 50.25(b)(5))
findings.verbatimText: Those subjects who are presently enrolled and actively participating in the study should be informed of the change if it might relate to the subjects' willingness to continue their participation in the study (21 CFR 50.25(b)(5)). FDA does not require reconsenting of subjects that have completed their active participation in the study, or of subjects who are still actively participating when the change will not affect their participation, for example when the change will be implemented only for subsequently enrolled subjects.

sources.title: Institutional Review Boards Frequently Asked Questions | FDA

findings.notes: An fda.gov result showed this text. I do not have the FAQ number. The FAQs are older (1998-era) Information Sheet guidance, but they were not among the documents the 2023 guidance says it supersedes.

findings.claim: In a search limited to fda.gov, one result said the IRB should decide whether enrolled subjects must be re-consented when a consent form is revised for a protocol change or new information. It also said FDA does not require re-consent for minor changes, though IRBs may require it.
findings.citation: FDA guidance on fda.gov, document not identified (probably the 2023 Informed Consent guidance FAQ section)
findings.verbatimText: Because the consent form is being modified to reflect changes to the protocol or new information, which may affect the willingness of already enrolled and actively participating subjects to continue in the clinical investigation, the IRB should determine the need to re-consent these enrolled subjects.
findings.notes: This came from a synthesized result of an fda.gov-only search. An exact-phrase search did not reproduce it, and I could not tell which fda.gov document it came from. Use it only as corroboration.

findings.claim: OHRP guidance treats giving new risk information to previously enrolled subjects as an action the IRB may need to consider after an unanticipated problem, next to revising the consent document. OHRP frames it as an IRB/investigator judgment, not an automatic rule.
findings.citation: OHRP, Reviewing and Reporting Unanticipated Problems Involving Risks to Subjects or Others and Adverse Events (January 15, 2007)
findings.verbatimText: modification of informed consent documents to include a description of newly recognized risks; provision of additional information about newly recognized risks to previously enrolled subjects
findings.notes: This is a list of examples of corrective actions 'that might need to be considered'. It is not a requirement. The guidance predates 2018, which is why it cites 46.116(b)(5).

findings.claim: SACHRP's recommendations of April 7, 2020 (Attachment A, 'New Information Provided to Previously Enrolled Research Subjects') say neither the Common Rule nor FDA regulations use the term 're-consent'. They recommend the least burdensome method for giving new information. SACHRP is an HHS advisory committee: its recommendations are not OHRP guidance and do not bind anyone.
findings.verbatimText: neither the Common Rule regulations nor the FDA regulations use the term "re-consent" or otherwise describe a process for approving the mechanism for providing new information to subjects

sources.title: Attachment A - New Information Provided to Previously Enrolled Research Subjects | HHS.gov

findings.notes: It is hosted on hhs.gov but is advisory, so do not cite it as OHRP guidance. An hhs.gov-limited search also showed 'the provision of new information should not automatically result in a process whereby subjects are expected to review and initial every page of the revised consent form' and 'IRBs should encourage use of the least burdensome approach'. That text is probably from this SACHRP document, but I could not confirm the attribution.

findings.claim: ICH E6(R2) 4.8.2 says three things. Revise the consent form when important new information becomes available. Get IRB/IEC approval of the revised form before using it. Inform subjects in a timely manner of new information relevant to their willingness to continue, and document that communication. It never uses the word 're-consent'.
findings.verbatimText: The written informed consent form and any other written information to be provided to subjects should be revised whenever important new information becomes available that may be relevant to the subject's consent. Any revised written informed consent form, and written information should receive the IRB/IEC's approval/favourable opinion in advance of use. The subject or the subject's legally acceptable representative should be informed in a timely manner if new information becomes available that may be relevant to the subject's willingness to continue participation in the trial. The communication of this information should be documented.
findings.notes: I pieced the sentences together from two results that each attributed them to 4.8.2. E6(R2) has been superseded by E6(R3).

findings.claim: In ICH E6(R3) (Step 4 final, 6 January 2025) the equivalent is 2.8.2. Participants must be informed in a timely manner of new information relevant to their willingness to continue. The communication, and the participant's confirmation of willingness to continue, must be documented. New information must be assessed to decide whether re-consent is needed, including whether it matters only to new participants or also to existing ones.
findings.verbatimText: The participant or the participant's legally acceptable representative should be informed in a timely manner if new information becomes available that may be relevant to the participant's willingness to continue trial participation ... The communication of this information and confirmation of the willingness to continue trial participation should be documented. ... New information that could impact a participant's willingness to continue participation should be assessed to determine if re-consent is needed (e.g., depending on the stage of the trial, consideration should be given to whether the new information is relevant only to new participants or to existing participants).

sources.title: E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice Guidance for Industry (FDA)

findings.notes: The primary PDFs came up for these phrases. The '2.8.2' number was tied to the text only through the ichgcp.net reproduction, a single secondary source. The (a)/(b)/(c) sub-lettering is lower still; see the next finding.

findings.claim: E6(R3) 2.8.2 appears to go on in lettered sub-items. (a) Assess whether re-consent is needed. (b) If it is needed (e.g., emerging safety concerns), clearly identify the new information in the revised consent materials. (c) Get IRB/IEC approval of revised consent materials before use.
findings.verbatimText: If re-consent is needed (e.g., information on emerging safety concerns), new information should be clearly identified in the revised informed consent materials. ... Revised informed consent materials should receive the IRB/IEC's approval/favourable opinion in advance of use.
findings.notes: The lettering came back only when my query contained it, so the result may just echo my query. The 2023 draft also came up, so the (c) sentence may come from the draft rather than the Step 4 final. Cite '2.8.2' without letters until someone checks the final PDF.

findings.claim: No change to approved research, including changes to the consent document, may start before IRB review and approval, except to eliminate apparent immediate hazards. For FDA-regulated research this is 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4).
findings.verbatimText: ensuring that changes in approved research, during the period for which IRB approval has already been given, may not be initiated without IRB review and approval except where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to the human subjects
findings.notes: The Common Rule counterpart the code cites, 45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii), came back with inconsistent wording in the search summaries. One summary mixed it with pre-2018 46.103(b)(4)(iii) text. Treat that designation as medium: it is probably correct, but I did not see its exact text.

findings.claim: 45 CFR 46.109(c) covers documentation of informed consent, not amendment or continuing review. Continuing review is 46.109(e).
findings.verbatimText: (c) An IRB shall require documentation of informed consent or may waive documentation in accordance with § 46.117. ... (e) An IRB shall conduct continuing review of research requiring review by the convened IRB at intervals appropriate to the degree of risk, not less than once per year, except as described in § 46.109(f).
findings.notes: Included because the header comment in protocol-amendments-logic.ts still cites 46.109(c) as 'continuing/amendment review'.

research.determination:
WHO DECIDES: the IRB. No US regulation uses the term 're-consent' or requires it automatically.
- 45 CFR 46.116(c)(5) (2018 rule; (b)(5) only for studies still under the pre-2018 rule) and 21 CFR 50.25(b)(5) are 'when appropriate' consent elements. They promise that significant new findings relating to willingness to continue will be provided.
- The IRB decides whether enrolled subjects get the new information and a chance to affirm continued participation, and by what method (revised consent form or an alternative such as an addendum or information sheet). Sources: 45 CFR 46.109(b) / 21 CFR 56.109(b), and FDA's final Informed Consent guidance (August 2023).
- ICH E6(R3) 2.8.2 (final 6 Jan 2025, replacing E6(R2) 4.8.2) likewise says new information 'should be assessed to determine if re-consent is needed'.

A deterministic engine may therefore report only indicators and who decides. It must never report 're-consent required' or 're-consent not required'. Rules:

R1. Replace `requiresReconsent: boolean|null` with a status enum and `decidedBy: 'IRB'`. The enum has no 'required' and no 'not_required' value, following the pattern of substantiality.ts, which never returns 'non-substantial'.

R2. affectsConsent === true OR affectsRisk === true gives status 'irb_determination_required'. The message: "The IRB determines whether currently enrolled, actively participating subjects must be given this information and an opportunity to affirm their willingness to continue, and by what method (revised consent document or an alternative such as an addendum or information sheet)." Citations: 45 CFR 46.116(c)(5); 21 CFR 50.25(b)(5); 45 CFR 46.109(b); 21 CFR 56.109(b); FDA Informed Consent guidance (Aug 2023); ICH E6(R3) 2.8.2.

R3. Otherwise, if either flag is null, status is 'undetermined' with settledBy naming the null field(s). Undeclared is not a No (the existing convention, kept).

R4. Both flags false gives status 'no_indicator_declared'. The message must say in words that this is not a determination that enrolled subjects need not be informed. The legal trigger is new information relevant to willingness to continue, which the two flags do not fully capture (e.g., added costs under 46.116(c)(3), or added visit burden). The IRB may still require the information under 46.109(b) / 56.109(b).

R5. amendmentType ('major' / 'minor' / 'administrative') must not change the re-consent status. The trigger is the effect of the new information on enrolled subjects, not the sponsor's label. Today 'major' with both flags false returns `false`, and so do 'minor' and 'administrative'.

R6. Whenever a consent impact is declared, emit this accompanying requirement: revised consent materials, or any addendum or information sheet, need IRB approval before use. Cite ICH E6(R2) 4.8.2 / E6(R3) 2.8.2, 21 CFR 56.108(a)(4), and 45 CFR 46.108(a)(3)(iii) (medium confidence on the exact text).

R7. The scope wording must say 'currently enrolled, actively participating subjects to whom the change applies'. Per FDA's IRB FAQs, FDA does not require re-consent of subjects who have completed active participation, or when a change applies only to subjects enrolled later. The engine has no subject-status data, so it states this scope and does not count subjects.

R8. Whatever the IRB decides, the engine may state one documentation duty: record the communication and the subject's confirmation of willingness to continue (ICH E6(R3) 2.8.2; E6(R2) 4.8.2).

R9. User-facing labels must read like 'IRB re-consent determination needed', never 'Re-consent'. The label must be derived from both affects_consent and affects_risk, not affects_consent alone.
codeDefects: server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:60,66 - `requiresReconsent: substantive ? true : ...` claims re-consent is REQUIRED whenever affectsConsent or affectsRisk is true. No regulation requires re-consent. Under 46.109(b)/56.109(b) and FDA's 2023 guidance, the IRB decides whether enrolled subjects are told the new information and by what method. A typo fix in the consent form, a lower risk, or a change applying only to future enrollees (FDA IRB FAQs) would all be wrongly flagged 're-consent required'. Should return an 'irb_determination_required' status.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:66 - for amendmentType 'major' with both flags false, returns `requiresReconsent: false`, a negative determination the engine cannot make. The sponsor's label does not decide re-consent. Should return 'no_indicator_declared'.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:74,76 - the minor/expedited and administrative branches return `requiresReconsent: false`. The regulatory trigger (46.116(c)(5)/50.25(b)(5): new findings that 'may relate to the subject's willingness to continue participation') is not the same as the two flags, and the IRB may still require information under 46.109(b)/56.109(b). Should return 'no_indicator_declared' with a message saying it is not a 'not required' determination.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:7 - the header cites '45 CFR 46.109(c) (continuing/amendment review)'. 46.109(c) is documentation of informed consent; continuing review is 46.109(e). The 2026-09-22 fix corrected FULL_BASIS but left this comment.

server/services/protocol-amendments/protocol-amendments-logic.ts:8 - '45 CFR 46.116 (re-consent when changes affect a subject's willingness to continue)' gets the rule wrong. 46.116(c)(5) is a 'when appropriate' consent element promising that significant new findings will be provided. It does not mandate re-consent. Cite 46.116(c)(5) / 21 CFR 50.25(b)(5) plus 46.109(b) / 56.109(b) for the IRB's authority.

The 'may' also contradicts the `requiresReconsent: true` returned with it.

The FAQ number for the FDA IRB FAQ quoted here.

Which studies remain under the pre-2018 Common Rule, where 46.116(b)(5) is the correct citation. My recollection is a general compliance date of 21 Jan 2019 with transition only by institutional election, but I did not verify it here.
The EU position (Regulation 536/2014) on informing or re-consenting participants after a substantial modification was not researched; this question was scoped to US and ICH.

findings.claim: Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 defines a 'substantial modification' as a change to any aspect of the trial, made after notification of an authorisation decision under Articles 8, 14, 19, 20 or 23, that is likely to have a substantial impact on subject safety or rights, or on the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the trial. The test is whether the change is likely to have that impact, not whether something changed.
findings.verbatimText: 'Substantial modification' means any change to any aspect of the clinical trial which is made after notification of a decision referred to in Articles 8, 14, 19, 20 or 23 and which is likely to have a substantial impact on the safety or rights of the subjects or on the reliability and robustness of the data generated in the clinical trial

sources.title: European Commission - Clinical Trial Regulation 536/2014: Changes to clinical trials (cites 'Art 2.2.13')

findings.notes: An exact-phrase search for this text returned results, and several independent secondary sources quoted it. A Commission-hosted presentation attaches it to 'Art 2.2.13', which is the same designation as Article 2(2)(13). The code's EU_DEF constant is correct.

findings.claim: Article 15 ('General principles', the first article of Chapter III) is what prevents implementation before approval. A substantial modification, explicitly including adding a trial site or changing the principal investigator at a site, may only be implemented once it has been approved under the Chapter III procedure.
findings.verbatimText: A substantial modification, including the addition of a clinical trial site or the change of a principal investigator in the clinical trial site, may only be implemented if it has been approved in accordance with the procedure set out in this Chapter.

sources.title: legislation.gov.uk - contents of 536/2014 (Chapter III, Article 15 'General principles')

findings.notes: The designation and substance are high confidence. Two exact-phrase segments matched EUR-Lex results: 'A substantial modification, including the addition of a clinical trial site or the change of a principal investigator' and 'may only be implemented if it has been approved'. The wording between them ('in' vs 'at' the clinical trial site, 'set out' vs 'laid down') comes from search-result text and was not checked word for word. Chapter III is titled 'Authorisation procedure for a substantial modification of a clinical trial'. This is the article to cite for 'requires authorisation before implementation', not Article 16.

findings.claim: Article 16 ('Submission of application') governs how the sponsor applies. The sponsor submits the application dossier for a substantial modification to the Member States concerned through the EU portal (CTIS), and the dossier's contents are set by Annex II. Article 16 does not contain the prior-authorisation rule (that is Article 15), and it does not contain any 'determination' of substantiality.

sources.title: CCMO - Submission of a substantial modification

findings.notes: The exact text of Article 16 was not seen. Search summaries mixed it up with Article 5 ('In order to obtain an authorisation, the sponsor shall submit an application dossier to the intended Member States concerned through the portal referred to in Article 80'), which covers initial applications. That Article 16 is the SM submission article, pointing to Annex II, is supported by the Chapter III structure and by NCA guidance saying the list of required SM documentation is in Annex II. This finding is enough to say Article 16 is the wrong citation for the implementation bar. It is not enough to quote Article 16.

findings.claim: Article 17 covers validation of an SM application that concerns only aspects covered by Part I of the assessment report (the protocol and the scientific or IMP documents). The Member States concerned may send the reporting Member State considerations on validation, and the reporting Member State validates.
findings.verbatimText: Validation of an application for the authorisation of a substantial modification of an aspect covered by Part I of the assessment report
findings.notes: The heading matched on an exact-phrase search against EUR-Lex and Lexparency. The day counts reported in the summaries (considerations within 5 days, validation within 6 days) were not seen verbatim, so they are medium confidence.

findings.claim: Article 18 covers assessment of a Part I substantial modification. The reporting Member State assesses it, including whether the trial will remain a low-intervention trial, and submits the final assessment report and conclusion through the EU portal within 38 days of the validation date.
findings.verbatimText: The reporting Member State shall assess the application with regard to an aspect covered by Part I of the assessment report, including whether the clinical trial will remain a low-intervention clinical trial after its substantial modification, and draw up an assessment report.
findings.notes: The text comes from a search summary drawn from EUR-Lex and legislation.gov.uk. The paragraph number inside Article 18 was not confirmed.

findings.claim: Article 19 covers the decision on a Part I substantial modification. Each Member State concerned notifies the sponsor through the EU portal, by a single decision, whether the SM is authorised, authorised subject to conditions, or refused.
findings.verbatimText: Each Member State concerned shall notify the sponsor through the EU portal as to whether the substantial modification is authorised, whether it is authorised subject to conditions, or whether authorisation is refused.

sources.title: European Commission - Changes to clinical trials (Articles 17-19 = Part I SM)

findings.notes: The Commission presentation says Part I SMs fall under Articles 17-19. One summary attached to Article 19 a time limit ('within five days from the reporting date or from the last day of the assessment period referred to in Article 22, whichever is later'). That wording belongs to Article 23. For Article 19, only 'within five days from the reporting date' is plausible, and it was not seen by itself. Tacit or deemed decisions were not researched.

findings.claim: Article 20 is a single article covering validation, assessment and decision for an SM that concerns only aspects covered by Part II of the assessment report. Examples of Part II aspects are subject information and consent, insurance, the trial site and the investigator. Each Member State concerned handles its own territory and first tells the sponsor, within six days, whether the SM concerns a Part II aspect and whether the dossier is complete under Annex II.
findings.verbatimText: Within six days from the submission of the application dossier, the Member State concerned shall notify the sponsor through the EU portal of whether the substantial modification concerns an aspect covered by Part II of the assessment report and whether the application dossier is complete in accordance with Annex II.

sources.title: CCMO - Validation and assessment of a substantial modification
European Commission - Changes to clinical trials (Article 20 = Part II SM, e.g. patient information, insurance, trial site, investigator)

findings.notes: The Article 20 heading, 'Validation, assessment and decision regarding a substantial modification of an aspect covered by Part II of the assessment report', matched on an exact-phrase search. The six-day text is from a summary of legislation.gov.uk and CCMO. Its paragraph number was not confirmed.

findings.claim: Articles 21 to 23 cover an SM that affects both Part I and Part II aspects. Article 21 has it validated under Article 17, with Part I aspects assessed under Article 18 and Part II aspects under Article 22. Article 22 has each Member State concerned assess the Part II aspects for its own territory within 38 days of validation. Article 23 requires a single decision per Member State.
findings.verbatimText: Where a substantial modification relates to aspects covered by Parts I and II of the assessment report, the application for authorisation of that substantial modification shall be validated in accordance with Article 17. ... The aspects covered by Part I of the assessment report shall be assessed in accordance with Article 18 and the aspects covered by Part II of the assessment report shall be assessed in accordance with Article 22.

sources.title: legislation.gov.uk - Article 23 'Decision on the substantial modification of aspects covered by Parts I and II'
European Commission - Changes to clinical trials (Articles 21-23 = Part I and II SM)

findings.notes: The first sentence of Article 21 matched an exact-phrase search on EUR-Lex. Article 22 text as summarised: 'Each Member State concerned shall assess, for its own territory, the aspects of the substantial modification which are covered by Part II of the assessment report and submit, through the EU portal, that report, including its conclusion, to the sponsor within 38 days from the validation date.' Article 23 text as summarised: 'Notification shall be done by way of a single decision within five days from the reporting date or from the last day of the assessment period referred to in Article 22, whichever is later.' The paragraph numbers inside Articles 21 to 23 were not confirmed. The brief described Articles 21-22 as the both-parts articles. The procedure actually runs across Articles 21, 22 and 23, and Article 24 (heading reported as 'Persons assessing the application for a substantial modification') closes Chapter III. Chapter III is therefore Articles 15-24.

findings.claim: Adding a Member State to an authorised trial is not a substantial modification. It is a separate application under Article 14, submitted to the additional Member State through the EU portal only after the initial authorisation decision. The reporting Member State stays the same, and the new Member State issues a single decision within 52 days.
findings.verbatimText: Where the sponsor wishes to extend an authorised clinical trial to another Member State ('additional Member State concerned'), the sponsor shall submit an application dossier to that Member State through the EU portal.
findings.notes: The exact phrase matched EUR-Lex and legislation.gov.uk's Article 14 page. The paragraph number (1) and the 52-day figure come from summaries, so they are medium confidence. Article 14 decisions are among those listed in the Article 2(2)(13) definition, which shows the Regulation treats adding a Member State as its own authorisation, not as an SM.

findings.claim: The sponsor must notify each Member State concerned through the EU portal of the end of the trial in that Member State, within 15 days of the end there. This is the mechanism for a trial that stops in one Member State.
findings.verbatimText: The sponsor shall notify each Member State concerned of the end of a clinical trial in relation to that Member State through the EU portal. That notification shall be made within 15 days from the end of the clinical trial in relation to that Member State.
findings.notes: The text was seen on an exact-phrase search. Paragraph (1) was not confirmed. Whether removing a Member State concerned before the trial starts there goes through Article 37 or through a CTIS withdrawal was not established.

findings.claim: A change that is not a substantial modification but is relevant to the Member States' supervision of the trial must be updated in the EU database (CTIS) by the sponsor on an ongoing basis. In CTIS and in NCA practice this is called an 'Article 81(9)' or '81.9' non-substantial modification.
findings.verbatimText: The sponsor shall permanently update in the EU database information on any changes to the clinical trials which are not substantial modifications but are relevant for the supervision of the clinical trial by the Member States concerned.

sources.title: European Commission - Clinical Trial Regulation 536/2014: Changes to clinical trials

research.determination:
Rules to implement, each tied to a finding:

R1 Definition, Art. 2(2)(13): a modification is substantial only if it is a change to an aspect of the trial made after an Art. 8/14/19/20/23 decision AND it is LIKELY TO HAVE A SUBSTANTIAL IMPACT on subject safety or rights, or on data reliability and robustness. The sponsor makes the classification (Q&A section 3 and NCA guidance). The engine can only report indicators. A changed field is evidence and not the classification, because the Q&A Annex IV lists protocol changes that are non-substantial. The output should say 'substantial-modification indicators present', not 'substantial'. Keep the existing refusal to output 'non-substantial'.

R2 Implementation bar, Art. 15: a substantial modification, explicitly including adding a trial site or changing a PI at a site, may only be implemented once approved under Chapter III (Arts 15-24). Cite Art. 15 for 'requires authorisation before implementation', never Art. 16.

R3 Submission, Art. 16 with Annex II: the SM application dossier (Annex II contents) goes to the Member States concerned through the EU portal (CTIS). Cite Art. 16 only for how and where to submit.

R4 Routing by assessment-report part:
- Part I aspects only (protocol design: endpoints, eligibility, intervention and dose, arms, statistics, randomisation and blinding, safety design; also IB and IMPD): Art. 17 validation, Art. 18 RMS assessment with the report within 38 days of validation, Art. 19 single decision per Member State.
- Part II aspects only (subject information and consent, insurance, site, investigator): Art. 20, where each Member State validates, assesses and decides for its own territory, with a 6-day completeness notification.
- Both parts (for example a protocol change that also changes the ICF): Art. 21 (validated per Art. 17; Part I assessed per Art. 18, Part II per Art. 22), Art. 22 (Part II assessment within 38 days), Art. 23 (single decision within 5 days of the reporting date or of the end of the Art. 22 period, whichever is later).
- Store the route as a computed field: part = I | II | I+II.

R5 Member-State scope changes are not SMs:
- Adding a Member State is an Art. 14(1) application to that additional Member State through the EU portal (single decision, reported as 52 days). It must not count toward an SM verdict.
- A trial ending in one Member State is an Art. 37 end-of-trial notification for that Member State within 15 days (medium confidence).
- A new SITE within an existing Member State concerned IS an SM under Art. 15 (Part II, Art. 20). Country-level region deltas cannot detect that.

R6 Non-substantial but relevant to supervision, Art. 81(9): the sponsor updates CTIS on an ongoing basis ('81.9 NSM'). Examples: an IB annual update with no benefit-risk change, sponsor or CRO contact changes. An 81.9 NSM is never a substitute for an SM.

R7 Other NSMs (neither substantial nor relevant to supervision): not notified in CTIS on their own. Record them in the TMF, list them in the cover letter of the next SM, and submit updated documents with that SM unless a condition requires otherwise (Q&A section 3 and Annex IV; medium confidence, from NCA-reported practice).

R8 Protocol-content citation: 'Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, Annex I, section D (Protocol)'. The itemised list is 'Annex I, section D, point 17'. Do not attach sub-letters for eligibility or endpoints until they are verified.

findings.claim: The FDA December 2024 draft guidance routes deviations as follows. Investigators report all protocol deviations to the sponsor. Investigators report important deviations, and changes made to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard, to the IRB (under 21 CFR 312.66 for drugs, 812.150(a)(4) for devices). Sponsors identify and report important deviations to FDA, for example in clinical study reports. As far as I recall it sets no severity-tiered day counts.

findings.notes: Recollection only. I could not confirm the section numbers, the exact recipients (for example whether all deviations or only important ones go to the IRB), or any timeframe wording such as 'promptly' or a day count. The one structural point I hold more firmly is that there is no 3-day or 10-day severity tier. That point is argued below from the regulations.

findings.claim: ICH E6(R2) 4.5.3 requires the investigator, or a person the investigator designates, to document and explain any deviation from the approved protocol. It contains no minor/major distinction and no statement that minor deviations are 'logged and summarized rather than promptly reported'. The code's reading of 4.5.3 is wrong.

The negative claim, that 4.5.3 has no minor-deviation carve-out, is what the product decision rests on, and it is supported by the secondary source. findings.claim: ICH E6(R2) 4.5.2 bars the investigator from implementing any deviation or protocol change without sponsor agreement and prior documented IRB/IEC approval. Exceptions: eliminating an immediate hazard to subjects, or changes that are only logistical or administrative. 4.5.4 lets the investigator make an immediate-hazard deviation without prior IRB approval. The deviation, its reasons and any proposed amendment then go as soon as possible to the IRB/IEC, the sponsor and, if required, the regulatory authorities.

findings.claim: ICH E6(R2) 5.20.1: noncompliance with the protocol, SOPs, GCP or regulations must lead to prompt sponsor action to secure compliance. Noncompliance that significantly affects, or could affect, subject protection or reliability of results requires root cause analysis and CAPA. 5.20.2: serious and/or persistent noncompliance by an investigator or institution leads to termination of their participation, and the sponsor promptly notifies the regulatory authorities. Neither clause is a deviation-reporting timeline.
findings.notes: Recalled. The code's phrase '§5.20 (prompt deviation reporting)' mischaracterizes the clause. The clause concerns sponsor handling of noncompliance, and the regulator notification it requires is triggered by terminating a site.

findings.claim: ICH E6(R3), Step 4 on 6 January 2025, carries these duties forward: the investigator documents and explains deviations, and makes no change without sponsor agreement and IRB/IEC approval except to eliminate an immediate hazard or for logistical/administrative changes. The sponsor noncompliance section keeps prompt action, root cause analysis and CAPA for significant noncompliance, and termination plus prompt notification for serious and/or persistent noncompliance. E6(R3) likewise sets no day counts for deviation reporting.

findings.claim: 21 CFR 312.66 (drugs): the investigator assures IRB review, promptly reports to the IRB all changes in the research activity and all unanticipated problems involving risk to subjects or others, and makes no changes without IRB approval except where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to subjects. The only timing word is 'promptly'.
findings.notes: Recalled. This text has been stable for decades. It supplies the investigator-to-IRB route for drug and biologic studies.

findings.claim: In 21 CFR 56.108, (a)(3) is IRB procedures for prompt reporting to the IRB of changes in research activity, and (a)(4) is ensuring changes are not started without IRB approval except to eliminate apparent immediate hazards. 56.108(b) is IRB procedures for prompt reporting to the IRB, institutional officials and FDA of: (b)(1) unanticipated problems involving risks to subjects or others; (b)(2) serious or continuing noncompliance with the regulations or IRB requirements or determinations; (b)(3) suspension or termination of IRB approval. Serious or continuing noncompliance is therefore 56.108(b)(2), not (b)(1).
findings.notes: Recalled. An earlier audit agent in this session reached the same structure independently: (a)(4) no changes without approval, (b) prompt reporting, (c) convened meetings. That agent was also working from memory. These are duties on the IRB's written procedures. Whether something is serious or continuing noncompliance is the IRB's determination, not a severity label the sponsor sets. No day count.

findings.claim: 21 CFR 812.150(a)(4) (devices): the investigator notifies the sponsor and the reviewing IRB of any deviation from the investigational plan made to protect the life or physical well-being of a subject in an emergency. The notice is due as soon as possible and no later than 5 working days after the emergency. Outside an emergency, the sponsor must approve changes or deviations in advance. If they may affect the plan's scientific soundness or subjects' rights, safety or welfare, FDA and IRB approval under 812.35(a) is also required.
findings.notes: Recalled. The window is 5 WORKING days, counted from the emergency. 812.150(a)(5) sets a similar 5-working-day report for using a device without informed consent. 812.150(a)(1), unanticipated adverse device effects, is 10 working days. That is the only 10-day window in this area, it covers adverse device effects and not deviations, and it may be where the code's '10' came from.

findings.claim: 45 CFR 46.108(a)(4) (2018 revised Common Rule): the IRB must set up and follow written procedures for prompt reporting to the IRB, institutional officials, the department or agency head and OHRP of (i) unanticipated problems involving risks to subjects or others, or serious or continuing noncompliance, and (ii) suspension or termination of IRB approval. 46.108(a)(3)(iii) covers changes not started without IRB approval except to eliminate apparent immediate hazards. Part 46 applies to HHS-conducted or HHS-supported research (46.101), not to an FDA-regulated industry trial as such. In the pre-2018 rule the same obligations were at 46.103(b)(4)-(5).
findings.notes: Recalled. This duty applies to the IRB/institution. It covers unanticipated problems and serious or continuing noncompliance, not every 'major' deviation. It sets no day count. For FDA-regulated trials the matching provisions are 21 CFR 56.108(b)(1)-(2), and 312.66 or 812.150(a)(4) for investigators.

findings.claim: OHRP guidance 'Reviewing and Reporting Unanticipated Problems Involving Risks to Subjects or Others and Adverse Events' (January 2007) reads 'prompt' for unanticipated problems as follows. Serious unanticipated problems go to the IRB within about 1 week of the investigator learning of them, other unanticipated problems within about 2 weeks, and IRB/institution reports to OHRP within about 1 month. This is non-binding guidance, covers unanticipated problems only (not protocol deviations generally), and applies within 45 CFR 46.
