RULES TO IMPLEMENT

R1. Severity is a human determination, so the system must not default it. Whether a deviation is important is decided for each trial from its design, critical procedures, data, subject protections and planned analyses (ICH E3 Q&A R1). FDA's Dec 2024 draft guidance has sponsors define important deviations in advance. The system cannot infer a severity.
- Severity is NULL or 'not_assessed' until a named, qualified user records severity, safety impact and a rationale. Those actions go in the audit trail.
- The UI must not preselect a severity.
- AnA must not supply severity as a finding. Under CLAUDE.md RULE 2 the model narrates and does not issue verdicts. A severity arriving through the tool is stored as unassessed, or as 'proposed', pending human confirmation.

R2. Safety impact is three-valued: true, false or unknown. Unknown is not false.

R3. An unassessed deviation must fail closed without inventing a verdict.
- Reportability is 'undetermined': not false, and not a fabricated true.
- Show 'Assessment required — reporting obligations cannot be determined until severity/importance is assessed.'
- Show a notice for each clock that could apply, counted from discovered_date:
  - EU trials: 7 days from sponsor awareness if the deviation turns out to be a serious breach (CTR Art 52).
  - UK trials: 7 days for a serious breach (reg 29A; verify post-28-Apr-2026).
  - Device emergency deviations: 5 working days after the emergency (812.150(a)(4)).
  - The IRB-of-record's configured policy window, if one is set.
- Block closure (the CAPA gate) until the deviation is assessed.
- Keep the deviation out of any 'non-reportable' count or summary.

R4. Replace the single 'reportable' boolean with obligations computed per route. Each route has a recipient, trigger, clock, clock unit and basis.
- (a) Investigator → sponsor, for every deviation, whatever its severity: document and explain it (ICH E6(R2) 4.5.3 / E6(R3) investigator section; FDA draft guidance: all deviations to sponsor). Drugs have no regulatory day count; the sponsor's protocol or plan sets it. Devices: emergency deviations within 5 working days (812.150(a)(4)); other device deviations need prior sponsor approval.
- (b) Investigator → IRB:
  - Drugs: promptly report changes in research activity and unanticipated problems. Make no change without IRB approval except to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard, then report it promptly (21 CFR 312.66; E6 4.5.4 'as soon as possible').
  - Devices: emergency deviations within 5 working days (812.150(a)(4)).
  - Which other deviations go to the IRB, and when, is set by the IRB's written procedures (21 CFR 56.108(a)(3)-(4), (b)). Store that as per-IRB configuration and label it 'IRB policy', never 'regulation'.
- (c) IRB/institution → FDA, and → OHRP/agency when the research is HHS-supported: promptly report unanticipated problems (56.108(b)(1); 46.108(a)(4)(i)), serious or continuing noncompliance (56.108(b)(2); 46.108(a)(4)(i)) and suspension or termination (56.108(b)(3); 46.108(a)(4)(ii)).
  - These determinations belong to the IRB. The sponsor platform may record them and must not compute them from severity.
  - Cite 45 CFR 46 only when the trial is flagged Common-Rule-covered.
- (d) Sponsor → FDA:
  - Drugs: no expedited per-deviation report. Important deviations go in the CSR (ICH E3 §10.2). Notify FDA if an investigator is terminated for noncompliance (312.56(b)).
  - Devices: FDA approval is needed for changes or deviations affecting scientific soundness or rights, safety or welfare (812.35(a)).
  - Anything further from the FDA draft guidance is a recommendation, and should be labelled 'FDA draft guidance (Dec 2024), nonbinding'.
- (e) Sponsor → EU Member States via CTIS: a serious breach within 7 calendar days of becoming aware (Reg 536/2014 Art 52(1)), using the Art 52(2) definition. This is a separate yes/no/undetermined decision, not the severity label.
- (f) Sponsor → MHRA: a serious breach within 7 days (SI 2004/1031 reg 29A; verify the post-28-Apr-2026 text).

R5. The '3 days critical / 10 days major' windows have no regulatory basis. Remove them. If an organization wants SOP windows, store them as configuration with the SOP reference, and have the basis read 'Organization SOP <ref>', never a CFR or ICH citation. Every clock carries its unit (calendar vs working days) and its anchor (discovery, sponsor awareness, or the emergency).

R6. Terminology: the regulatory classes are important / not important (ICH E3, FDA). 'Serious breach' (EU/UK) and 'serious or continuing noncompliance' (IRB) are separate determinations. Minor/major/critical may remain as an internal scale, but it must map explicitly to 'important' and must not be presented as a regulatory category.

R7. Legacy data: existing rows written with the 'minor' default cannot be told apart from rows genuinely assessed as minor. The governed-action ledger payload also recorded the defaulted value. Migrate them to 'not_assessed' unless there is independent evidence of assessment, following the precedent of the amendment fix in 3495d6c4f. Under CLAUDE.md RULE 1, change the default by amending migrations/20260629_protocol_deviations.sql in place, with a dated header note. Do not append a DROP.

research.determination:
VERDICT ON THE LABEL. "The un-disableable Part 11 invariant" is not accurate. Part 11 does not require the signer to be someone other than the author. 11.50(a)(3) lists "authorship" as a signature meaning, so Part 11 expects authors to sign their own records (findings 1-2). Author-not-equal-approver is a predicate-rule and governance control. Its explicit sources are record-specific: 211.186(a) (master production and control records independently checked by a second person), 211.194(a)(8) (second-person lab record review), 211.22/211.100(a)/211.192 (QCU review and approval), 58.35(a) (GLP QAU independence) and ISO 13485 8.2.4 via 820.10. The platform adopts the rule in its governance contract. Part 11's role is enforcement: 11.10(g) authority checks and 11.10(f) sequencing checks (findings 3, 8-12). Keep the control un-disableable as platform policy; the label is what is wrong. Suggested header: "Separation of duties (four-eyes) for review, approval and lock. Platform governance control implementing predicate-rule independence (21 CFR 211.186(a), 211.194(a)(8), 211.22, 211.100(a), 211.192; 58.35(a); ISO 13485:2016 via 21 CFR 820.10), enforced as a Part 11 authority check (21 CFR 11.10(g)) and operational check (11.10(f)). Authorship is established from the audit trail (11.10(e)); signatures carry their meaning (11.50(a)(3)). Not itself a Part 11 requirement." Do not cite 11.200(a)(3) for this rule; it is anti-impersonation (finding 7).

RULES FOR ENGINEERS.
R1 (scope by meaning; findings 1, 3). Apply the check to signatures whose declared 11.50(a)(3) meaning is review, approval, responsibility or release (REVIEWER/APPROVER/review/approval/release), and to `lock`. Do not refuse an AUTHOR/authorship signature because the signer is the author; that is the case 11.50(a)(3) describes. If a `sign` has no declared meaning, treat it as approval-class, which fails closed.

R2 (authorship is a set drawn from immutable sources, not one mutable column; findings 5, 15, 16). For the version being signed, the authors are every user who created or changed its content, drawn from:
